[Cabernet Sauvignon](/wiki/Cabernet_Sauvignon "Cabernet Sauvignon") grapes in [Médoc](/wiki/M%C3%A9doc_AOC "Médoc AOC")

Red Bordeaux is generally made from a blend of grapes. Permitted grapes are [Cabernet Sauvignon](/wiki/Cabernet_Sauvignon "Cabernet Sauvignon"), [Cabernet Franc](/wiki/Cabernet_Franc "Cabernet Franc"), [Merlot](/wiki/Merlot "Merlot"), [Petit Verdot](/wiki/Petit_Verdot "Petit Verdot"), [Malbec](/wiki/Malbec "Malbec") and [Carménère](/wiki/Carm%C3%A9n%C3%A8re "Carménère").[[14]](#cite_note-Brook_36-74-14) Today Carménère is rarely used, with [Château Clerc Milon](/wiki/Ch%C3%A2teau_Clerc-Milon "Château Clerc-Milon"), a [fifth growth](/wiki/Bordeaux_Wine_Official_Classification_of_1855 "Bordeaux Wine Official Classification of 1855") Bordeaux, being one of the few to still retain Carménère vines. As of July 2019, Bordeaux wineries authorized the use of four new red grapes to combat [effects of climate change on viticulture](/wiki/Effects_of_climate_change_on_agriculture "Effects of climate change on agriculture") in Bordeaux, though only for those wines designated as Bordeaux or Bordeaux Supérior. These newly approved grapes are [Marselan](/wiki/Marselan "Marselan"), [Touriga Nacional](/wiki/Touriga_Nacional "Touriga Nacional"), [Castets](/wiki/Castets_(grape) "Castets (grape)"), and Arinarnoa.[[15]](#cite_note-:0-15)[[16]](#cite_note-16)

As a broad generalisation, Cabernet Sauvignon (Bordeaux's second-most planted grape variety) dominates the blend in red wines produced in the Médoc and the rest of the left bank of the [Gironde estuary](/wiki/Gironde_estuary "Gironde estuary"). fanoutqa_028733.t: Italian campaign (World War II) :: part 05 :: chunk_0004
fanoutqa_028733.x:
Italian campaign (World War II) :: part 05 :: chunk_0004
The **Italian campaign** of [World War II](/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), also called the **Liberation of Italy** following the [German occupation](/wiki/Operation_Achse "Operation Achse") in September 1943, consisted of [Allied](/wiki/Allies_of_World_War_II "Allies of World War II") and [Axis](/wiki/Axis_powers "Axis powers") operations in and around [Italy](/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy "Kingdom of Italy"), from 1943 to 1945. The joint [Allied Forces Headquarters](/wiki/Allied_Force_Headquarters "Allied Force Headquarters") (AFHQ) was operationally responsible for all Allied land forces in the [Mediterranean theatre](/wiki/Mediterranean_and_Middle_East_theatre_of_World_War_II "Mediterranean and Middle East theatre of World War II") and it planned and led the [invasion of Sicily](/wiki/Allied_invasion_of_Sicily "Allied invasion of Sicily") in July 1943, followed in September by the [invasion of the Italian mainland](/wiki/Allied_invasion_of_Italy "Allied invasion of Italy") and the campaign in Italy until the [surrender](/wiki/Surrender_of_Caserta "Surrender of Caserta") of the [Axis forces](/wiki/Axis_powers "Axis powers") in Italy in May 1945.

Chad Hurley :: Early life and education :: chunk_0001
Chad Meredith Hurley was born on January 24, 1977 in [Reading, Pennsylvania](/wiki/Reading,_Pennsylvania "Reading, Pennsylvania"). He is the second child of Don and Joann Hurley, and he grew up near [Birdsboro, Pennsylvania](/wiki/Birdsboro,_Pennsylvania "Birdsboro, Pennsylvania").[[7]](#cite_note-7) He has an older sister, Heather, and a younger brother, Brent.[[8]](#cite_note-8)

Since childhood, Hurley showed interest in the arts, and became interested in computers and electronic media during high school.[[9]](#cite_note-9) He was a standout runner for Twin Valley High School's cross-country program, which won two of its PIAA State titles with him as a member in 1992 and 1994. He was also a member of the [Technology Student Association](/wiki/Technology_Student_Association "Technology Student Association") during high school. He graduated from [Twin Valley High School](/wiki/Twin_Valley_High_School_(Pennsylvania) "Twin Valley High School (Pennsylvania)") in 1995 and earned a [BA](/wiki/Bachelor_of_Arts "Bachelor of Arts") in [Fine Art](/wiki/Fine_art "Fine art") from [Indiana University of Pennsylvania](/wiki/Indiana_University_of_Pennsylvania "Indiana University of Pennsylvania") in 1999.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

In 1751, Franklin and [Thomas Bond](/wiki/Thomas_Bond_(American_physician) "Thomas Bond (American physician)") obtained a charter from the Pennsylvania legislature to establish a hospital. [Pennsylvania Hospital](/wiki/Pennsylvania_Hospital "Pennsylvania Hospital") was the first hospital in the colonies.[[79]](#cite_note-82) In 1752, Franklin organized the [Philadelphia Contributionship](/wiki/Philadelphia_Contributionship "Philadelphia Contributionship"), the Colonies' first [homeowner's insurance](/wiki/Home_insurance "Home insurance") company.[[80]](#cite_note-83)[[81]](#cite_note-84)

Between 1750 and 1753, the "educational triumvirate"[[82]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOlsen2013174-85) of Franklin, [Samuel Johnson](/wiki/Samuel_Johnson_(American_educator) "Samuel Johnson (American educator)") of [Stratford, Connecticut](/wiki/Stratford,_Connecticut "Stratford, Connecticut"), and schoolteacher [William Smith](/wiki/William_Smith_(Episcopal_priest) "William Smith (Episcopal priest)") built on Franklin's initial scheme and created what [Bishop James Madison](/wiki/James_Madison_(bishop) "James Madison (bishop)"), president of the [College of William & Mary](/wiki/College_of_William_%26_Mary "College of William & Mary"), called a "new-model"[[83]](#cite_note-86) plan or style of American college. Franklin solicited, printed in 1752, and promoted an American textbook of [moral philosophy](/wiki/Ethics "Ethics") by Samuel Johnson, titled *Elementa Philosophica*,[[84]](#cite_note-87) to be taught in the new colleges. In June 1753, Johnson, Franklin, and Smith met in Stratford.[[85]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEOlsen2013163–274-88) They decided the new-model college would focus on the professions, with classes taught in English instead of Latin, have subject matter experts as professors instead of one tutor leading a class for four years, and there would be no religious test for admission.[[86]](#ci

The earliest published discovery of a moon other than Earth's was by [Galileo Galilei](/wiki/Galileo_Galilei "Galileo Galilei"), who discovered the four [Galilean moons](/wiki/Galilean_moons "Galilean moons") orbiting [Jupiter](/wiki/Jupiter "Jupiter") in 1610. Over the following three centuries, only a few more moons were discovered. Missions to other planets in the 1970s, most notably the *[Voyager 1](/wiki/Voyager_1 "Voyager 1")* and *[2](/wiki/Voyager_2 "Voyager 2")* missions, saw a surge in the number of moons detected, and observations since the year 2000, using mostly large, ground-based [optical telescopes](/wiki/Optical_telescope "Optical telescope"), have discovered many more, all of which are irregular.

On several occasions, NCAA tournament teams have played their games in their home arena. In 1959, Louisville played at its regular home of [Freedom Hall](/wiki/Freedom_Hall "Freedom Hall"); however, the Cardinals lost to [West Virginia](/wiki/1958%E2%80%9359_West_Virginia_Mountaineers_men%27s_basketball_team "1958–59 West Virginia Mountaineers men's basketball team") in the semifinals. In 1984, Kentucky defeated Illinois, 54–51 in the Elite Eight on its home court of Rupp Arena. Also in 1984, #6 seeded Memphis played the first two rounds on its home court, defeating Oral Roberts and Purdue. In 1985, Dayton played its first-round game against Villanova (it lost 51–49) on its home floor. In 1986 (beating Brown before losing to Navy) and '87 (beating Georgia Southern and Western Kentucky), Syracuse played the first 2 rounds of the NCAA tournament in the Carrier Dome. Also in 1986, LSU played in Baton Rouge on its home floor for the first 2 rounds despite being an 11th seed (beating Purdue and Memphis State). In 1987, Arizona lost to UTEP on its home floor in the first round. In 2015, [Dayton](/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_Dayton_Flyers_men%27s_basketball_team "2014–15 Dayton Flyers men's basketball team") played at its regular home of [UD Arena](/wiki/UD_Arena "UD Arena"), and the Flyers beat [Boise State](/wiki/2014%E2%80%9315_Boise_State_Broncos_men%27s_basketball_team "2014–15 Boise State Broncos men's basketball team") in the First Four.
